surfaces.name: Array
surfaces.stdout:
# The one sequence — SPEC.md, "0.1.0", item 3.
#
# `Array` is a compiler-known generic class, like `String`: an array literal is
# lowered to `Array(T).unsafe_build` and `to_unsafe` before any of this is
# read (`LiteralExpander#expand`), so those two names are not ours to choose.
#
# A buffer, a size and a capacity. Growth doubles, which is the only policy
# that keeps a run of `<<` linear, and there is no shrinking; `shift` steps
# the buffer forward, so the capacity is what is left past it.
class Array(T)

  # The two in order, as a new array; neither operand changes.
  def +(other : Array(T)) : Array(T)

  def <<(value : T) : Array(T)

  def ==(other : Array(T)) : Bool

  # A negative index counts from the end, so `a[-1]` is the last element.
  # Still out of range after that wrap (or empty) raises, same message.
  def [](index : Int32) : T

  def []=(index : Int32, value : T) : T

  def []?(index : Int32) : T | ::Nil

  def all?(& : (T -> Bool)) : Bool

  def any?(& : (T -> Bool)) : Bool

  # The elements that are not nil, in an array whose type says so: what a
  # list of `to_i?` answers becomes once the failures are dropped.
  def compact

  # `a.concat(a)` is a doubling, not a loop: `each` walked *other*'s growing
  # size while `<<` grew it, so `[1, 2].concat(itself)` grew the buffer until
  # the capacity arithmetic overflowed. The length is read once.
  def concat(other : Array(T)) : Array(T)

  # The questions a list gets asked with one answer. `find` answers nil
  # when none does, the way Crystal's does and `index` below already did.
  def count(& : (T -> Bool)) : Int32

  # Every element equal to `value` out, answering the last or nil, as the
  # other library's: it took the first alone, `[1, 2, 1]` left `[2, 1]`.
  def delete(value : T) : T | ::Nil

  def dup : Array(T)

  def each(& : (T -> Nil)) : Nil

  def each_with_index(& : (T, Int32 -> Nil)) : Nil

  def empty? : Bool

  def find(& : (T -> Bool)) : T | ::Nil

  # The first `n`, or all of them when there are fewer: a prefix, not a
  # question, so it never panics.
  def first(n : Int32) : Array(T)

  # `first` on an empty array is a mistake rather than a nil: the array knows
  # it is empty and so does whoever wrote the call. `last?` above answers the
  # other question, and is the one the trait defaults use.
  def first : T

  # Hashing follows `==`, mixed as a tuple's members are (object.iyi): an
  # array writes `==`, so `Reference#hash` answered its type's id and every
  # array key shared one slot - 40,000 of them took 1.2 s to insert.
  def hash : Int32

  def includes?(value : T) : Bool

  # Where a value first is, or nil.
  def index(value : T) : Int32 | ::Nil

  def inspect : String

  def join(separator : String) : String

  # Here rather than on `Enumerable`: the trait is iyi's, written in
  # `src/std`, and every one of its methods that returns a sequence
  # returns one of these. So an `Array` is what a sample ends up holding, and
  # `join` is what it ends up calling.
  # With nothing between: `["a", "b"].join` is `"ab"`.
  def join : String

  # `last` on an empty array is a mistake rather than a nil, as `first` is.
  def last : T

  def last? : T | ::Nil

  def map(& : (T -> U)) : Array(U) forall U

  # The element whose key is largest, or smallest, the first of equals; a
  # NaN key is above every other, as `<=>` places it. Empty is a mistake.
  def max_by(& : (T -> U)) : T forall U

  def min_by(& : (T -> U)) : T forall U

  def new(capacity : Int32)

  def new

  # Removes and returns the last element. Empty is a mistake, as with `last`.
  def pop : T

  def reduce(initial : U, & : (U, T -> U)) : U forall U

  def reject(& : (T -> Bool)) : Array(T)

  # A copy in the other order.
  def reversed : Array(T)

  def select(& : (T -> Bool)) : Array(T)

  # Removes and returns the first element. The buffer steps past it rather
  # than the rest moving down: moving them made draining a queue quadratic,
  # and `while item = queue.shift?` - how the prelude says a queue is
  # drained - took 1.6 s over 100,000 items. The slot stepped past is still
  # the buffer's chunk, which the collector keeps by the pointer into it,
  # and the next growth copies only what is left.
  def shift : T

  # The first element or nil, which is how a queue is drained: `while
  # item = queue.shift?`.
  def shift? : T | ::Nil

  def size : Int32

  def sort_in_place(& : (T, T -> Int32)) : self

  # The pair for elements that already compare, by `<`. SPEC.md III.1.7a
  # pairs `sort_in_place` with `sorted` and the hint for `sort!` names both,
  # but only `sorted` had this form: "expected to be invoked with a block".
  def sort_in_place : self

  # Sorted on a key each element answers, ascending by `<`: the same pair
  # as above, one name longer. Each element's key is computed once, and the
  # pairs of key and element are what the merge sort orders.
  def sort_in_place_by(& : (T -> U)) : self forall U

  # The copy, with the comparison written out. One body, because the difference
  # between the pair is which array it runs on. The block is handed on through
  # `yield`, not captured: a captured block is kept to call later, and `!` in
  # it was refused as "maybe by a task" although the sort runs it here.
  def sorted(& : (T, T -> Int32)) : Array(T)

  def sorted : Array(T)

  def sorted_by(& : (T -> U)) : Array(T) forall U

  # The sum of the elements, and `T.zero` (src/iyi/number.iyi) when there
  # are none, as `std/enumerable`'s `sum` answers: this one raised "sum of
  # an empty array" where `Set(Int32).new.sum` was 0. `["a", "b"].sum` is a
  # compile error, as in the other library; `join` puts strings together.
  def sum : T

  # The sum of what the block answers for each element, and the block's
  # own zero when there are none.
  def sum(& : (T -> U)) : U forall U

  # `[1, 2, 3]`, the way it is written: an array printed is its elements
  # inspected, so a string inside keeps its quotes and a nil says so. Cast,
  # or `Tuple.new.to_a`'s `Array(NoReturn)` "can't infer block return type".
  def to_s : String

  # The same values as a `Set`, in the order first met.
  def to_set : Set(T)

  def to_unsafe : Pointer(T)

  # Each value once, in the order first met, found through a table: a
  # search of what was kept so far made it quadratic, 284 ms for 200,000
  # elements with 10,000 distinct.
  def uniq : Array(T)

  # :nodoc:
  def unsafe_set_size(size : Int32) : Nil

  # Pairs, element by element, as many as this array holds: a shorter
  # *other* is refused at its first missing index, as the other library does.
  def zip(other : Array(U)) : Array(Tuple(T, U)) forall U

  # The same pairs handed to a block, with no array of them made: the
  # other library's `a.zip(b) { |x, y| ... }`, which a training loop calls
  # a few million times, and which refuses a shorter *other* the same way.
  def zip(other : Array(U), & : (T, U -> _)) : Nil forall U

  # `Array.new(729, 0)`: *size* copies of *value*, the other library's fill
  # form. A second argument used to be an arity error beside a one-argument
  # form that means capacity, which a port reads as the fill it was.
  def self.new(size : Int32, value : T) : Array(T)

  # `Array(T).new(n) { |i| ... }`: n elements, each the block's answer for
  # its index - a row of a grid, a table of squares.
  def self.new(size : Int32, & : (Int32 -> T)) : Array(T)

  # An array of *capacity* elements that are not written yet. The literal
  # expander fills them through `to_unsafe` immediately afterwards, which is
  # why this is allowed to hand out a size it has not stored anything at.
  def self.unsafe_build(capacity : Int32) : Array(T)
end

surfaces.name: Atomic
surfaces.stdout:
# iyi: `Atomic(T)` — a word two threads may both write. SPEC.md III.4.10.
#
# The first thing in this prelude that assumes a second thread, and it
# arrived the way everything here arrives, with a caller: the thread
# floor (`bench/thread_floor.iyi`) counted its threads in and out on
# three `fun`s of inline asm, and the release build's `xchg` clobbered a
# register the asm had declared an input, which cost a day. These six
# verbs are the compiler's own instructions instead — `atomicrmw`,
# `cmpxchg`, an ordered load and an ordered store — so the register
# allocation is LLVM's problem, the aarch64 arm is whatever the target's
# CPU offers (`ldaxr`/`stlxr` loops, or LSE's `ldaddal` where the
# machine has it), and nothing is spelled twice per architecture. The
# floor holds: `nm -u` on a program that uses one names nothing new,
# because a 64-bit-or-narrower atomic is an instruction on every target
# iyi links for, never a `__atomic_*` call. `bench/thread_floor.sh`
# asserts that, plain and release, on both Linux arms and on darwin.
#
# **One ordering, sequentially consistent, and no parameter to weaken
# it.** This is Go's rule (its memory model makes every `sync/atomic`
# operation sequentially consistent and the package has no ordering
# argument) rather than C++'s or Rust's, and it is a decision, not an
# omission. An ordering parameter is the part of an atomic API people
# get wrong, the compiler cannot check, and a program cannot test for;
# the cost of not having it is a fence on the architectures that
# distinguish the orderings, and on x86_64 — the machine the floor was
# measured on — a sequentially consistent `add` and a relaxed one are
# the same `lock xadd`. On aarch64 the difference is `ldaddal` against
# `ldadd`, and it is not yet a number: the day a profile of the marker
# or the scheduler names one, that measurement is what adds the
# weaker spelling, and it will be added as its own verb rather than a
# parameter, so a call site says what it means.
#
# `T` is one of the four integers `primitives.iyi` gives arithmetic to.
# A pointer or a reference is refused by name rather than admitted
# untested: the arena list that will want one is the caller that will
# bring it. The verbs and their answers are Crystal's, so a program that
# reads the same under `--crystal` means the same: `add`, `sub` and
# `swap` answer the value the word held before; `compare_and_set`
# answers that value and whether the exchange happened, which is what a
# retry loop needs without a second load.
#
# An `Atomic(T)` is a struct holding the word, so it lives where it is
# declared — a class's field, a class variable, a mapping — and the
# instructions address that word in place. Copying one copies a number,
# not a synchronisation, which is the same contract Crystal's has.
struct Atomic(T)

  # `word += value`; answers what the word held before.
  def add(value : T) : T

  # If the word holds `expected`, it now holds `desired`. Answers what the
  # word held, and whether the exchange happened; a retry loop feeds the
  # first back in as its next `expected`.
  def compare_and_set(expected : T, desired : T) : Tuple(T, Bool)

  # The word, read once, ordered.
  def get : T

  def new(value : T)

  # The word, written once, ordered.
  def set(value : T) : Nil

  # `word -= value`; answers what the word held before.
  def sub(value : T) : T

  # `word = value`; answers what the word held before.
  def swap(value : T) : T
end

surfaces.name: Channel
surfaces.stdout:
# ── Channel — III.4.6 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# `Channel(T).new` is a rendezvous, as Crystal's is: a send completes when
# a receive takes it, and either side parks until the other arrives. A
# parked sender carries its value in its node's box, and a parked
# receiver has a slot a sender fills, so the handoff needs no third
# party; `new(capacity)` buffers that many sends first. Closing drains
# what was delivered, then refuses: a parked sender whose box is still
# full failed, and its value dies with the node.
#
# `T : Share` is not enforced yet for the reason the file header gives:
# one thread cannot race, and a marker that gates nothing cannot be
# tested for gating. `select` is answered by this protocol — a node per
# arm, one nonce, losers stale by arithmetic until the woken select takes
# them out — at the bottom of the class.
class Channel(T)

  # Everyone parked is woken; what each wake means is read on the woken
  # side — a receiver finds the buffer, then `ChannelClosed`; a sender
  # finds its box still full.
  def close : Nil

  def closed? : Bool

  def new(capacity : Int32)

  def new

  # `select`'s arms park through these with one shared nonce; a plain
  # call parks with a fresh nonce of its own. *slot* is where a rendezvous
  # sender puts its value (`IyiWaiter#slot`).
  def park_receive_node(fiber : IyiFiber, nonce : UInt64, slot : UInt64) : IyiWaiter

  def park_send_node(fiber : IyiFiber, nonce : UInt64, value : T) : IyiSendNode(T)

  # Assumes `send_ready?`. A rendezvous puts the value in the parked
  # receiver's own slot (`hand`). It went into the buffer, and the send
  # answered delivered on the word of the wake: a select woken that way
  # took another arm ready by then, a receiver cancelled before it ran
  # answered `Cancelled`, and either way the value stayed in a channel of
  # no capacity after its sender left. A buffered send completes when the
  # buffer takes it, so there the woken receiver finds it in the buffer.
  def put_now(value : T) : Nil | ChannelClosed

  # A closed channel drains what was delivered before it refuses. A
  # rendezvous sender that finds this receive parked writes its value into
  # `got` and marks the node handed, and that is the answer even when the
  # task was cancelled before it ran: the sender was told it was taken.
  # A woken park that was handed nothing takes its node out of the queue,
  # so a cancelled one leaves nothing behind.
  def receive : T | ChannelClosed | Cancelled

  def receive_ready? : Bool

  # Nothing happens on the arm `take_now` answers: `ChannelClosed` is
  # the refusal here, where a closed channel's buffer is spent.
  def receive_refused? : Bool

  def receive_select_action : IyiReceiveSelect(T)

  def send(value : T) : Nil | ChannelClosed | Cancelled

  def send_ready? : Bool

  def send_select_action(value : T) : IyiSendSelect(T)

  # Assumes `receive_ready?`: the buffer, then a parked sender's box,
  # then the refusal.
  def take_now : T | ChannelClosed

  # Out of the receive queue from wherever it stands, in constant time,
  # and no longer linked anywhere; a node no queue holds is left as it
  # is. The queue is linked both ways because a select's losing arms
  # leave from the middle: they stayed until something walked them off
  # the head, so a loop selecting over a busy channel and an idle one
  # left a node in the idle one's queue for every park - 30 MiB kept
  # after two million rounds, freed only when the idle channel was used.
  def unlink_receiver(node : IyiWaiter) : Nil

  # The send queue's `unlink_receiver`.
  def unlink_sender(node : IyiSendNode(T)) : Nil

  # No arm ready answers -1, which the expansion's case meets with the
  # program's own `else`.
  def self.non_blocking_select(actions : U, bound : Int32) forall U

  # ── select — III.4.6, the library half of the expansion ────────────
  #
  # A `select` compiles to `%i, %v, %h = ::Channel.select({arm, arm}, b)`
  # and a case over the index; `non_blocking_select` when an `else` arm
  # exists. One def serves every arity, because a tuple's size is a
  # compile-time fact a macro walks. `%h` says the arm's operation
  # happened, and an arm nobody binds runs its body only then: it ran
  # unless its answer was an `Error`, so a `Channel(Boom)`'s receive took
  # the `Boom` and skipped the body. *bound* is the first arm that binds,
  # -1 for none, and a cancelled task's `Cancelled` goes to it, as that
  # arm's own primitive would have answered it.
  def self.select(actions : U, bound : Int32) forall U
end

surfaces.stdout:
# One character - a byte, in this prelude, which reads its strings as ASCII.
struct Char < Value

  def !=(other : Char) : Bool

  # The character *other* code points on: what `'a'..'z'` steps by. `chr`
  # refuses a surrogate too, where `'\u{D7FF}' + 1` was U+D800.
  def +(other : Int32) : Char

  def <(other : Char) : Bool

  def <=(other : Char) : Bool

  def ==(other : Char) : Bool

  def >(other : Char) : Bool

  def >=(other : Char) : Bool

  def alphanumeric? : Bool

  def bytesize : Int32

  def digit? : Bool

  # `0x10FFFF` is the last code point there is; past it a `'?'` goes out
  # rather than a sequence no reader can decode. `String::Builder` writes
  # these too, which had its own copy of the four arms.
  def each_byte(& : (UInt8 -> Nil)) : Nil

  def hash : Int32

  def inspect : String

  # Itself as `inspect` writes it between *quote*s, the other library's
  # escapes; not `printable?`, as `\u` and hex. `'\''` was `'''`.
  def inspect_into(io : String::Builder, quote : Char) : String::Builder

  # The classes a word counter asks about, ASCII's: a letter is one of the
  # fifty-two, a digit one of the ten. Whitespace is the other library's:
  # the space and `\t` to `\r`, and above ASCII Unicode's Zs, Zl and Zp, so
  # U+00A0 and U+3000 are and U+0085, a control, is not. It was ASCII's.
  def letter? : Bool

  def ord : Int32

  # Not a control (Cc), format (Cf) or private-use (Co) character of
  # Unicode 15, nor whitespace but the space: the other library's.
  def printable? : Bool

  def to_s : String

  def whitespace? : Bool
end

surfaces.name: Enum
surfaces.stdout:
# What an `enum` can do — SPEC.md, "0.1.0", item 3.
#
# The compiler gives an enum exactly two methods: `value`, the integer the
# member was numbered with, and `new`, which wraps one (`EnumType#initialize`).
# Everything a program does with an enum is the library's, and until
# `samples/iyi/enums.iyi` asked there was none of it — so the answers were
# `Object`'s: `Level::Warn == Level::Warn` was **false**, `to_s` printed the
# type's name, and `case level when Level::Warn` matched nothing, because a
# `when` naming a member lowers to `Level::Warn === level` and `===` is `==`.
# The compiler's own per-member question methods (`level.warn?`) call that
# same `==`, and a `@[Flags]` enum's call `includes?`, so those were broken by
# one gap apiece.
#
# `Enum` is predefined — it is what every enum's ancestor is, created before a
# prelude line is read — so this reopens it the way `Range` and `String` are
# reopened rather than declaring it.
#
# Read off the type at each instantiation: a method here is stencilled onto the
# enum that calls it, so `@type` is that enum and `@type.constants` are its
# members. Nothing walks a table at run time and nothing is allocated to answer
# a name: `to_s` is a `case` over integers the compiler folds.
struct Enum < Value

  def &(other : self) : self

  # An order, because a level is a threshold: `level >= Level::Info` is the
  # first thing a program writes after a `case`. Four operators rather than a
  # `Comparable` include — the prelude has no such module, and a trait would be
  # `std/traits`' to carry (SPEC.md II.6).
  def <(other : self) : Bool

  def <=(other : self) : Bool

  # Equality is the value's, which is what makes every other name work: `!=`
  # and `===` are `Object`'s and both read this, `case` lowers to `===`, and
  # the question methods the compiler writes are `self == Member`.
  def ==(other : self) : Bool

  def >(other : self) : Bool

  def >=(other : self) : Bool

  # A key in a `Hash` is hashed and then compared, so a type used as one owes
  # both (`src/iyi/hash.iyi`). The value's own hash: `to_i32` panicked past it.
  def hash : Int32

  # Whether every bit of *other* is in this one, which is what a `@[Flags]`
  # enum's question methods ask: the compiler writes `mode.read?` as
  # `self.includes?(Mode::Read)`.
  def includes?(other : self) : Bool

  # `#{Level::Warn.inspect}` is the member written down rather than printed,
  # and for an enum the two are the same text. It is here because `Object`'s
  # sends it back to `to_s` — which was the type's name — and a sample that
  # inspects a `Level?` was reading that.
  def inspect : String

  # The member's name, and the value's digits where no member has it —
  # `Level.new(9).to_s` is `"9"`, which is what a value off a wire prints as.
  #
  # A flags enum answers with a member's name when one has its value (`None`
  # for zero, `All` for every bit, which was skipped), else the names of the
  # bits it holds, each named once, and the rest as a number: `Read | 8`.
  def to_s : String

  # The two set operators a flags enum is built to be used with. `Mode::Read |
  # Mode::Write` is how one is written down, and `mode & Mode::Write` is how a
  # bit is taken out of it.
  def |(other : self) : self

  # A member from the integer it was numbered with, or `nil` where no member
  # has it. `new` takes any value of the base type by design — that is how an
  # enum comes back from C or off a wire — and this is the question that asks
  # whether the one in hand is a member.
  def self.from_value?(value : Int) : self | ::Nil

  # The same list said in text, which is what a message naming the choices
  # needs: `"one of #{Level.names.join(", ")}"`.
  def self.names : Array(String)

  # A member read back from text, or `nil` where no member has that name. What
  # a program does with an argument or a configuration line, so the comparison
  # is the lenient one a person types: `"warn"`, `"Warn"` and `"WARN"` all
  # answer `Level::Warn`, and nothing else does.
  #
  # `nil` rather than a panic, because the text is somebody else's input and
  # the caller is the only thing that knows what to say about it (III.1).
  def self.parse?(name : String) : self | ::Nil

  # Every member, in the order they were written. A menu, a validation table,
  # a loop that has to reach all of them — and for a flags enum the members
  # rather than `None` and `All`, which are the compiler's own.
  def self.values : Array(self)
end

surfaces.name: Hash
surfaces.stdout:
# The one dictionary — SPEC.md, "0.1.0", item 3.
#
# Two dense arrays in insertion order, keys and values, and an index over
# them: open addressing with linear probing from the key's hash to the
# position of its entry, `-1` where a slot is free. The compact layout
# Python's dictionary and the other library's `Hash` both settled on:
# iteration follows the order things went in - the order a word count
# prints its words - and the index is one array of integers rather than a
# copy of the keys. Deletion marks the entry gone and its index slot a
# tombstone, `-2`, which a probe steps over and an insert may take; the
# dense arrays close their gaps when they next grow. Closing the gap at
# once and rebuilding the index emptied a set of 20,000 in 0.95 s.
#
# Hashing is `key.hash`, defined per type in this prelude, and not iyi's
# `Hashable` trait: that lives in `src/std`, the opt-in library, and a
# prelude that depended on it would have the dependency backwards.
class Hash(K, V)

  def [](key : K) : V

  def []=(key : K, value : V) : V

  def []?(key : K) : V | ::Nil

  # The value the key had, or nil. The entry is marked gone where it
  # stands, so the order of what remains is the order it went in, and its
  # index slot becomes a tombstone. `each` starts past the gone at the
  # front: from entry 0, taking the oldest key and deleting it until none
  # was left stepped over every one gone before, 197 ms for 40,000.
  def delete(key : K) : V | ::Nil

  # Every pair, in the order it went in.
  def each(& : (K, V -> Nil)) : Nil

  def empty? : Bool

  def has_key?(key : K) : Bool

  def inspect : String

  # The keys, and the values, each in the order they went in.
  def keys : Array(K)

  def new

  def new(&block : (Hash(K, V), K -> V))

  def size : Int32

  # Every pair as a tuple, in the order it went in - what a sort by value
  # starts from.
  def to_a : Array(Tuple(K, V))

  # `{"a" => 1}`, in insertion order, both sides inspected; a first key in
  # braces is spaced off, `{ {1, 2} => 3 }`, as a tuple's: `{{` is a macro.
  def to_s : String

  def values : Array(V)

  def self.new(default : V) : Hash(K, V)
end

#
# **This is iyi's list, not Crystal's.** `src/primitives.cr` declares twelve
# numeric types and crosses them with each other, which is 2,580 definitions
# expanded on every build and **0.11 s of a 0.17 s front end** — measured by
# deleting the block and building again. iyi crosses five, which is 445.
#
# The five are `Int32`, `Int64`, `UInt8`, `UInt64` and `Float64`: the default
# integer, the one a byte count grows into, the byte itself, the one an address
# and a size are, and a float. `UInt16` joins them for comparison alone, for
# the reason written at the cross below: a wide character is compared on
# every Windows path. `Int8`, `Int16`, `Int128` and the unsigned middle exist
# as types and have no arithmetic, because no sample writes one — the same
# rule the rest of the prelude is built on. Writing `1_i8 + 1_i8` is an
# "undefined method" and that is the honest answer: 0.1.0 does not have
# eight-bit arithmetic rather than having it slowly.
#
# **Comparison is not refused the same way, and that is a defect this file
# cannot close.** `Object#==` answers `false` for anything no type claimed,
# which is right about two objects and a lie about two numbers: without
# `import std/int`, `1_i8 == 1_i8` is `false` rather than an error, and it
# was `92_u16 == 92_u16` answering false that hid two Windows defects for a
# week. Refusing it needs both sides' types at once, which a method body
# does not have — a guard on the receiver alone refuses `5 == nil`, where
# `false` is the correct answer, and it was measured doing exactly that to
# eleven exercises. The fix belongs in overload resolution, where the
# compiler knows both types; until then `UInt16` being in the cross is what
# the library's own callers needed, and this paragraph is the rest of the truth.
class Object

  def !=(other) : Bool

  def ==(other) : Bool

  # Case equality, what a `when` asks of each arm: equality, unless a type
  # answers with something stronger - a range, a class, a tuple.
  def ===(other) : Bool

  def class

  # Every type is usable as a `Hash` key, and one that has not said how it
  # hashes hashes to its type: correct and useless, every value of the type
  # in one slot, the honest default. A type used as a key defines `hash`.
  def hash : Int32

  # `value.in?(a, b)` — the Kemal port's way of writing an alternation. On
  # `Object` because it is about the value, not about any one type of it.
  def in?(*values : *T) : Bool forall T

  # What a value looks like written down rather than printed: the two differ
  # for `nil` and strings, and `#{value.inspect}` shows a value is absent.
  def inspect : String

  # The type's own name, which is what a value that has said nothing about
  # itself can honestly print. A type that wants better defines its own.
  def to_s : String
end

surfaces.name: Pointer
surfaces.stdout:
# A raw address: `Pointer(T).malloc(n)` is `n` elements of untyped memory,
# `[]` and `[]=` read and write them, nothing checks the bounds.
struct Pointer(T) < Value

  def +(offset : Int64) : self

  def -(other : self) : Int64

  def [](offset : Int32) : T

  def []=(offset : Int32, value : T) : T

  def address : UInt64

  # Bytes, not elements: every caller here is copying string contents.
  def copy_from(source : Pointer(T), count : Int32) : Nil

  def new

  def realloc(size : UInt64) : self

  def value : T

  def value=(value : T)

  def self.malloc(size : UInt64)

  def self.new(address : UInt64)
end

surfaces.name: Program
surfaces.stdout:
# The running program: its arguments and its environment, on demand.
class Program

  # The arguments after the program's own name, the way every shell
  # hands them over.
  def self.args : Array(String)

  # The directory the process is in, which is not what `PWD` says.
  # `PWD` is a variable a shell keeps: cmd and PowerShell never set it,
  # so on Windows every program that expanded a relative path panicked
  # ("no base given and PWD is not set"), and on POSIX it is a copy that
  # a program's own `Dir.cd` leaves behind. Nil when the platform has no
  # answer — wasm32-wasi resolves a path against a preopened directory
  # and names none — or when the directory is gone from under the
  # process.
  #
  # 4096 bytes covers POSIX's PATH_MAX and Windows' MAX_PATH; the second
  # try is for a Windows path built with `\\?\`, which reaches 32,767
  # characters and up to three UTF-8 bytes each.
  def self.cwd : String | Nil

  # One variable, or nil. No map of everything: the asking program names
  # what it wants, and a tool that dumps its whole environment into a
  # structure was one `puts` away from leaking it.
  def self.env(name : String) : String | Nil
end

surfaces.name: Range
surfaces.stdout:
# Ranges — SPEC.md, "0.1.0", item 3.
#
# The compiler expands a range literal to `Range.new(from, to, exclusive)`
# (literal_expander.cr) and predefines the type to refer to it; with no
# methods, `(1..10).each` was refused with "wrong number of arguments for
# 'Range(B, E).new'", a constructor nobody wrote. A range here counts up by
# one and stops: no `Enumerable`, no `step`, no reverse iteration.
struct Range(B, E)

  # A range is a value, so two written the same way are the same range:
  # `Object#==` is identity, and `(1..3) == (1..3)` was false. `1..3` and
  # `1...3` differ, and that is the flag's whole job.
  def ==(other : self) : Bool

  # `when 1..5` is `(1..5) === x`: inclusion. `==` answered, and no arm matched.
  def ===(value) : Bool

  def begin : B

  # The inclusive walk stops *at* the end rather than stepping past it: with
  # `value <= @end` the last step left the type on the checked `+`, so
  # `(2147483645..2147483647).each` panicked with "arithmetic overflow" at
  # the value it was asked to yield last.
  def each(& : (B -> Nil)) : Nil

  def end : E

  # `1...10` excludes its end, `1..10` includes it.
  def exclusive? : Bool

  # And hashing follows equality, or equal ranges would land in two slots.
  def hash : Int32

  # The three a range is written for: a value per position, the positions
  # that answer, and the total.
  def map(& : (B -> U)) : Array(U) forall U

  def new(begin __arg0 : B, end __arg1 : E, exclusive : Bool)

  def select(& : (B -> Bool)) : Array(B)

  def size : Int32

  def sum : B

  def to_a : Array(B)

  # `1..5` and `1...3`, each end inspected and a nil one left out, as the
  # other library writes one; `Object#to_s` printed `Range(Int32, Int32)`.
  def to_s : String
end

surfaces.name: Reference
surfaces.stdout:
# What every class instance is: a pointer to its fields, compared and
# hashed by identity unless the class says otherwise.
#
# That was this comment's promise and nothing kept it: `Object#==` answers
# false, so an instance was not even equal to itself, and a `Set(Node)`
# never found the node just added to it nor a `Hash(Node, V)` its key.
# Identity is `==` now, and the hash is the address. A class that writes
# its own `==` says what equal means, and the address would part two
# instances it calls equal - so one that writes `==` and no `hash` keeps
# the type's id, correct for any `==` and one slot for every instance, the
# default `Object#hash` explains.
class Reference

  def ==(other : Reference) : Bool

  def hash : Int32

  def new

  def object_id : UInt64
end

surfaces.name: Set
surfaces.stdout:
# The one set — "have I seen this", with nothing attached to the answer.
#
# A `Hash` whose values are nothing: the same dense keys in insertion
# order and the same index over them, so `add`, `includes?` and `delete`
# cost what the hash's do and iteration reads back in the order things
# went in. It is a wrapper rather than a copy of `hash.iyi` because the
# index is the part worth getting right once. The sample that asked for
# it (`samples/iyi/visited.iyi`) walks a graph with a cycle in it, and
# `add` answering whether the element was new is the one bit that walk
# needs.
class Set(T)

  # Not in `other`, in this order; `other` may be of another element type.
  def -(other : Set(U)) : Set(T) forall U

  # True when the element was not there before.
  def add(value : T) : Bool

  # True when the element was there.
  def delete(value : T) : Bool

  # Every element, in the order it went in.
  def each(& : (T -> Nil)) : Nil

  def empty? : Bool

  def includes?(value : T) : Bool

  def inspect : String

  def new

  def size : Int32

  def to_a : Array(T)

  # `Set{"a", "b"}`, in insertion order, elements inspected.
  def to_s : String
end

surfaces.name: String
surfaces.stdout:
# Text — SPEC.md, "0.1.0", item 3.
#
# The compiler declares `String`'s fields itself — `@bytesize`, `@length` and
# `@c`, in that order, in `Program#initialize` — because codegen lays out
# string literals before any prelude is read. So this file reopens a type that
# already has its shape and only says what can be done with it.
class String

  # `"ab" * -3` answered `""` where the other library raises (III.1.7a).
  # The size is a division, so the refusal names the string: `"abcd" *
  # 600_000_000` panicked "arithmetic overflow", the machine's adder.
  def *(count : Int32) : String

  def +(other : String) : String

  # Byte order, which for ASCII is dictionary order with the capitals first;
  # a prefix sorts before what it prefixes. What `sorted` and `sorted_by`
  # ask of a string.
  def <(other : String) : Bool

  # Thirty-two bytes a step while they last, then one at a time, and the
  # same string is itself: a byte a step was eleven times Python's `==`,
  # 230 ms for 1,000 compares of equal megabytes. No load needs alignment.
  def ==(other : String) : Bool

  # A negative *start* counts from the end, the same wrap as the one-index
  # form. *count* stays non-negative: a negative count is not a wrap, it is a
  # mistake, and it raises for that reason rather than being silently clamped.
  def [](start : Int32, count : Int32) : String

  # The character at *index*, asked for by `samples/iyi/calc`, which scans
  # its input a character at a time. Byte-indexed: a byte is the character
  # for ASCII, and `each_char` is the decoded walk. A negative index counts
  # from the end; out of range after that wrap raises, `[]?` answers nil.
  def [](index : Int32) : Char

  def []?(index : Int32) : Char | ::Nil

  # Where *search* first starts at or after byte *offset* - counted from
  # the end when negative - in bytes, as Crystal's `byte_index` answers.
  # Naive while that is cheap, and Rabin-Karp - one rolling hash per
  # position, bytes compared only where it matches - once more than four
  # bytes a position have been compared: a needle that keeps almost
  # matching, `"a" * 1000 + "b"` in a run of `a`, made the naive loop
  # n * m, 222 ms for a megabyte.
  def byte_index(search : String, offset : Int32 = 0) : Int32 | ::Nil

  def bytesize : Int32

  # `'\n'` is a line's end, so it takes the `\r` before it, or a lone `\r`
  # in its place, as the other library's does: `"a\r\n".chomp('\n')` is "a".
  def chomp(char : Char) : String

  # The other half of `upcase`, ASCII for the same reason.
  def downcase : String

  # Every character in order, decoded, as many as `size` counts: it yielded
  # one per byte, so `"héllo".size` was 5 and `each_char` ran six times.
  # Indexing stays byte-indexed (`[]` above), as `samples/iyi/calc` scans.
  # A byte that begins no character is one U+FFFD, as in the other library:
  # a lead byte took the bytes after it whatever they were, C3 41 was the
  # one character U+00C1, and `"a" C3 '"'` swallowed the quote.
  def each_char(& : (Char -> Nil)) : Nil

  def empty? : Bool

  def ends_with?(suffix : String) : Bool

  # FNV-1a over the bytes: three lines, no table, and good enough for a
  # linear-probing table of a few dozen entries.
  def hash : Int32

  def includes?(other : String) : Bool

  # Where a character first is, or nil: the question a parser asks before
  # it cuts.
  def index(char : Char) : Int32 | ::Nil

  # The literal that spells it, escaped as the other library's, a byte that
  # is no UTF-8 as `\x`: unescaped, `["a\", \"b"]` printed as two strings.
  def inspect : String

  def lchop(char : Char) : String

  # The lines of a text, blank ones included, a final newline ending the last
  # line; `\r\n` ends one too, and a last `\r` with no `\n` after it is kept:
  # `"1\r\n".lines[0].to_i` panicked where `File.read_lines` read 1.
  def lines : Array(String)

  def ljust(width : Int32, pad : Char = ' ') : String

  # Pad on the left (rjust) or the right (ljust) to *width*, in characters
  # as `size` counts them, the pad as its own bytes: in bytes,
  # `"héllo".rjust(7, '.')` answered a string of `size` 6, and a `'·'`
  # written as one byte left a lone continuation byte in the result.
  def rjust(width : Int32, pad : Char = ' ') : String

  # A zero `@length` on a non-empty string is "not counted yet", which is
  # how the other library's own code leaves a string it builds: `to_json`'s
  # result answered `size` 0 here while the field was returned as it stood.
  # The layout is shared on purpose (SPEC.md Part V item 12), so the
  # invariant is too. The count is of what `each_char` yields, a byte that
  # begins no character one U+FFFD.
  def size : Int32

  # The pieces between separators, empty ones included: `"a,,b".split(',')`
  # is three, `"a,".split(',')` is two, and `"".split(',')` is one empty
  # piece - the count the other library gives, so a program reads the same
  # under both.
  def split(separator : Char) : Array(String)

  # The three the Kemal port's path joining needs, byte-indexed: the same
  # as by character while the strings are ASCII.
  def starts_with?(prefix : String) : Bool

  # A `Char` above ASCII is more than one byte, and these narrowed it to one
  # through a *checked* convert, so `"a☃b".index('☃')` died of "arithmetic
  # overflow". Each compares the character's own bytes now.
  def starts_with?(char : Char) : Bool

  # Without `Char#whitespace?`'s characters at either end, decoded: it read
  # bytes, and `"b\u00A0".strip` kept the space the other library takes.
  def strip : String

  # The double nearest the decimal written here, correctly rounded: the
  # digits and the exponent are read into the printer's bignum and the
  # quotient taken to 54 bits with a sticky remainder, so what `to_s`
  # wrote reads back as the same double, every time, and "0.1" is the
  # double the literal `0.1` is. Accepts `-1.5`, `2.5e-3`, `1E10`, `.5`,
  # `7.`, `Infinity`, `NaN`, with `Char#whitespace?` around as `to_i?`
  # takes it; raises "not a number" for anything else.
  def to_f : Float64

  # The number this string spells - an optional sign and decimal digits,
  # the whole string - as `samples/iyi/calc` reads a token. Raises on
  # anything else, as the other library's does (SPEC.md III.1.7a): a
  # silent 0 for `"oops"` is wrong twice; `to_i?` answers nil for it.
  def to_i : Int32

  # Around the digits, `Char#whitespace?` is skipped as the other
  # library's `whitespace: true` skips it (`"42\n".to_i?` was nil). Read
  # as a *negative* magnitude, which holds every value the type has:
  # `2147483648` accumulated and negated, `Int32::MIN` overflowed on its
  # last digit, a panic rather than the `nil` a `?` promises.
  def to_i? : Int32 | ::Nil

  def to_s : String

  def to_unsafe : Pointer(UInt8)

  # ASCII only, and the samples are ASCII. A prelude that folded case for
  # every alphabet would be a Unicode table, which is more lines than this
  # whole file and not what any sample is about.
  def upcase : String

  def self.build(capacity : Int32 = 64, & : (String::Builder -> _)) : String

  # Interpolation is a call the compiler writes: `"a#{b}"` reaches here as
  # `String.interpolation("a", b)` (`LiteralExpander#expand`). The overloads
  # are what let the common shapes avoid work — a single string is itself.
  def self.interpolation(value : String) : String

  def self.interpolation(value) : String

  def self.interpolation(*values : *T) : String forall T

  # Allocates *bytesize* bytes, hands the buffer to the block to fill, and
  # returns the string that results. The character count is left at zero,
  # "not counted yet", for `size` to scan the first time it is asked: most
  # strings built here - an encoding, a join, a line - are never asked, and
  # counting them all was a second pass over every byte built.
  #
  # The byte after the last is a NUL, as a literal's is, so `to_unsafe` is
  # a C string: `std/process` and `std/debug` hand one to the platform as a
  # path. The byte was allocated for that and never written, and a string's
  # chunk is atomic - not cleared - so a chunk that had held a longer
  # string kept that string's byte there. Measured on Windows after a
  # collection that freed longer strings: 961 of 1,000 strings built after
  # it had no terminator, and `Process.run` of a path built that way
  # answered "no such program" for a file that was there.
  def self.new(bytesize : Int32, & : (Pointer(UInt8) -> Nil)) : String
end

surfaces.name: Struct
surfaces.stdout:
# A struct is its fields, as the other library's `Struct#==` has it: two are
# equal when each field is. `Object#==` answers false, so a struct was not
# equal to itself - `b == b` was false and `{b => 1}[b]?` nil. `Object#hash`
# stays correct for it, one slot a type; a struct that is a key writes one.
struct Struct < Value

  def ==(other : self) : Bool
end

surfaces.name: Tuple
surfaces.stdout:
# A tuple written the way it is written: `{1, "a"}`. The compiler lays a
# tuple out and answers `[]`; what it looks like printed is the prelude's,
# one element per position, each inspected.
tuple Tuple(*T) < Value

  # Two tuples are the same value when their members are. `Object#==` is
  # false, so `{1, 2} == {1, 2}` was, and a tuple key was never found in a
  # `Hash`. Member by member where one type holds the other, so `case {1,
  # y} when {1, 2}` (y : Int32?) matches; `{-1}` and `{-1_i64}` are unequal.
  def ==(other : Tuple(*U)) : Bool forall U

  # Each member's own `===`: `when {Nil, Bool}` holds for `{nil, false}`,
  # which `==` - a class against a value - never did.
  def ===(other : Tuple(*U)) : Bool forall U

  # Indexed by a *value* rather than by a literal, which is what walking a
  # tuple at runtime needs: `std/indexable`'s `values_at` and `sprintf` do.
  def [](index : Int32)

  # And hashing follows equality: a key is found by its slot first and
  # compared second, and `Object#hash` put every tuple in one slot. Each
  # member multiplied through and its high bits folded back down: `a * 31 +
  # b` gave the million points of a 1,000 by 1,000 grid 32,000 hashes, and
  # a table probing a slot at a time had not filled in ten minutes.
  def hash : Int32

  def inspect : String

  # How many: the type's own arithmetic, here rather than in `format.iyi`,
  # where `std/indexable` could only reach it with a formatter compiled in.
  def size : Int32

  # A first member in braces of its own is spaced off, `{ {1, 2}, 3 }`, as the other library's is.
  def to_s : String
end

  def compare_and_set_acquire(expected : T, desired : T) : Tuple(T, Bool)

  # `expected` it now holds `desired`; answers what the word held and

  def compare_and_set_release(expected : T, desired : T) : Tuple(T, Bool)
  # A full fence: nothing crosses it in either direction.

  # Both halves, without the total order of `fence`.

  # Nothing after this fence moves before it.

  # Nothing before this fence moves after it.
  def self.fence_release : Nil
  # The word, read once; nothing after the read moves before it.
  def get_acquire : T
  # The word, read once, atomic and nothing more.
  def get_relaxed : T
  # `word = max(word, value)`, signed or unsigned as `T` is; answers what

  # `word = min(word, value)`, signed or unsigned as `T` is; answers what
  # the word held before.

  # The word, written once; nothing before the write moves after it.

  # is not keeps all `precision` digits, so the reader sees where it was cut.

# shape is libc's, so the callers above read the same; a failure comes
# back as the negative errno the kernel answers, which every caller
# here reads as "not zero". `realpath` is a walk over `readlinkat` and
# `newfstatat`, since libc's is a library function and not a call.

    def initialize

  # branches (nested to ten), and `\` the next character literally. Only
  # `/` in the pattern matches a separator. On Windows a name's `\` is a
  # separator as well, and a pattern's `\` is one too rather than an
  # escape: `Dir.glob` answers with either.

  # research.swtch.com/glob), linear in the name but for braces. This
  # had `*` and `?` alone, byte by byte: `*` crossed separators, `?` took
  # half of a two-byte character, `[a]` and `{a,b}` were literal text,

  # after. The name was the process id and a counter, and the file was
  # written wherever the path led if nothing was there when asked: a
  # symlink planted at the next name in a shared `/tmp` between the
  # question and the write sent an upload wherever its owner pointed it.

  # cannot be planted in advance either; Windows' `%TEMP%` belongs to the
  # user, and there the create's refusal is the guarantee and the name

  def self.tempfile(prefix : String = "tmp", suffix : String = "", &block : (String -> Nil)) : Nil

  # `Int64` second and an `Int32` microsecond padded to eight, so four
  # `Int64` slots are the two structures and the odd slots are the
  # microseconds, zero.
  def self.touch(path : String | Path, time : Int64 = 0_i64) : Nil

  def self.writable?(path : String | Path) : Bool

module std/format

# The argument list as one array or tuple, as `sprintf` takes it.
pub def printf(format_string : String, args : Array) : Nil

pub def printf(format_string : String, args : Tuple) : Nil

pub def printf(format_string : String, *args : *T) : Nil forall T

# The argument list may be one array or tuple, as the other library takes
# it: `"%s, %s, %s, D" % ['A', 'B', 'C']`, its own example, panicked "too
# few arguments for format string" here, and `"[%s]" % ["A"]` printed
# `[["A"]]` where it prints `[A]`. Two overloads rather than one taking
# `Array | Tuple`: a union with Array in it cannot be written into an
# artifact ("can't use Array(T) in unions yet").
pub def sprintf(format_string : String, args : Array) : String

pub def sprintf(format_string : String, args : Tuple) : String

pub def sprintf(format_string : String, *args : *T) : String forall T

class ::IyiBig
  # self / small for a `small` under 2^32, self reduced to the quotient,
  # the remainder answered. A limb is 32 bits in a 64-bit word, so the
  # running remainder shifted up by a limb still fits the word.
  def div_small(small : UInt64) : UInt64
  # Base ten, most significant digit first, nine digits per division.
  def to_decimal : String
end

module ::IyiFloatText
  # Extracts Dragon4 digits for a non-zero, finite double.
  # Returns {digits_pointer, count, k} where value = 0.d1 d2 ... dn * 10^k.
  def self.dragon4(value : Float64) : ::Tuple(Pointer(UInt8), Int32, Int32)
  # Scientific notation with exact places, half to even.
  def self.format_exp(value : Float64, uppercase : Bool, precision : Int32, hash_flag : Bool) : String
  # Fixed-point decimal format with exact places, half to even.
  def self.format_fixed(value : Float64, precision : Int32) : String
  # a * b as its high and low words, from 32-bit halves.
  def self.mul_wide(a : UInt64, b : UInt64) : ::Tuple(UInt64, UInt64)
  # Every digit the double has, not the shortest ones padded with zeros:
  # `round(f * 2^e * 10^places)`, half to even, as decimal digits. This is
  # what a fixed or scientific format prints, and what it did not print:
  # `%.0f` of 1e23 answered 100000000000000000000000 where the double is
  # 99999999999999991611392, `%.20f` of 0.1 answered twenty zeros where
  # the value's digits are 0.10000000000000000555, and `%e` of the
  # smallest denormal answered 5.000000e-324 for 4.940656e-324 - the
  # shortest digits, which round-trip, are not the value, and past them
  # there was nothing but zeros. `places` may be negative, a scale down.
  def self.scaled_digits(f : UInt64, e : Int32, places : Int32) : String
  # `scaled_digits` in two words, when they hold it: f * 10^places is
  # under 2^117 for the places a word of ten's powers reaches, and the
  # quotient by 2^-e and its half-to-even rounding are shifts and one
  # comparison of the remainder with the half. The same integer the
  # bignum's division gives - it is the same arithmetic, exact - where
  # that division made `%.2f` three times what Go's takes. nil when the
  # value, the places or the answer do not fit.
  def self.scaled_quick(f : UInt64, e : Int32, places : Int32) : UInt64 | ::Nil
end

module ::IyiFormat
  # Any integer: an `Int64` or a `UInt64`, whose top half `to_i64` refuses.
  def self.code_point(code) : Char
  # A width or a precision, which an `Int32` holds: read into one, the
  # digits of `%99999999999d` panicked "arithmetic overflow".
  def self.field_number(format_string : String, start : Int32, stop : Int32, what : String) : Int32
  def self.format_arg(val, verb : Char, minus : Bool, plus : Bool, space : Bool, zero : Bool, hash : Bool, width : Int32, precision : Int32) : String
  # A number is a code point, as Crystal's `%c` has it: `%c` of 233 is
  # `é`, where it panicked "233 is out of char range" (`chr` is ASCII).
  # Anything else is its first character, not its first byte, which cut
  # `é` in half.
  def self.format_char_arg(val, minus : Bool, width : Int32) : String
  # Digits as `to_s(base)` writes them, a `-` first when negative, given
  # the verb's sign, prefix, precision and width.
  def self.format_digits(text : String, verb : Char, base : Int32, minus : Bool, plus : Bool, space : Bool, zero : Bool, hash : Bool, width : Int32, precision : Int32) : String
  def self.format_float64(val : Float64, minus : Bool, plus : Bool, space : Bool, zero : Bool, hash : Bool, width : Int32, precision : Int32) : String
  def self.format_float_exp(val : Float64, uppercase : Bool, minus : Bool, plus : Bool, space : Bool, zero : Bool, hash : Bool, width : Int32, precision : Int32) : String
  # `%g`: the shorter of the two notations, C's rule. With P the precision
  # (6 when none is given, 1 when it is 0) and X the exponent `%e` would
  # write at P - 1 places, it is `%e` at P - 1 places when X < -4 or X >= P
  # and `%f` at P - 1 - X places otherwise; either way the trailing zeros
  # of the fraction go, and its point with them, unless `#` keeps them.
  # NaN and the infinities are written as `%e` writes them.
  def self.format_float_general(val : Float64, uppercase : Bool, minus : Bool, plus : Bool, space : Bool, zero : Bool, hash : Bool, width : Int32, precision : Int32) : String
  def self.format_int64(val : Int64, base : Int32, uppercase : Bool, signed : Bool, minus : Bool, plus : Bool, space : Bool, zero : Bool, hash : Bool, width : Int32, precision : Int32) : String
  # Width and precision in characters, because `size` is and because
  # `%-10s` is a column: counted in bytes, a multi-byte string came out
  # short by one space per extra byte, and a precision cut a character in
  # half. The prelude's `ljust`/`rjust` decided the same thing.
  #
  # The characters a precision keeps are written into one buffer, as
  # `each_char` decodes them and `size` counts them: added one at a time
  # onto a string of their own, the text was copied once per character,
  # and `%.800000s` of a megabyte took 12.8 s, four times as long for
  # every doubling.
  def self.format_string_arg(str : String, minus : Bool, width : Int32, precision : Int32) : String
  # A float under an integer verb is truncated, which is what Ruby, Python
  # and the other language answer to it. Past an `Int64` the truncation is
  # the double's own integer, f * 2^e, written whole as Python writes it:
  # `%d` of 1e30 is 1000000000000000019884624838656, where `to_i64`
  # panicked "arithmetic overflow". NaN and the infinities have no
  # integer, and the refusal says that rather than "arithmetic overflow".
  def self.format_truncated(val : Float64, verb : Char, minus : Bool, plus : Bool, space : Bool, zero : Bool, hash : Bool, width : Int32, precision : Int32) : String
  def self.format_uint64(val : UInt64, base : Int32, uppercase : Bool, signed : Bool, minus : Bool, plus : Bool, space : Bool, zero : Bool, hash : Bool, width : Int32, precision : Int32) : String
  # An `Int128` or `UInt128`: an integer verb writes its digits, which may
  # not fit 64 bits; a float verb its nearest double, as `%f` of an
  # `Int64` is.
  def self.format_wide(val, verb : Char, minus : Bool, plus : Bool, space : Bool, zero : Bool, hash : Bool, width : Int32, precision : Int32) : String
  # A numeric verb is a claim about the argument, and an argument that is
  # not a number contradicts it: `%d` of "abc" printed abc, `%f` of a
  # `Char` printed the character, and the caller who had mistyped the
  # argument order saw their strings where their numbers should be and
  # nothing said so.
  def self.not_a_number(val, verb : Char) : NoReturn
  # A decimal's fraction without its trailing zeros, and without its point
  # when nothing is left after it: `%g`'s trim.
  def self.trim_fraction(text : String) : String
end

  def %(args : Tuple) : String

surfaces.stdout:
module std/gc

pub struct GC
  # What the collector can answer, read at one instant.
  struct Stats
    # Bytes the last sweep handed back, and bytes it found still live.
    def bytes_freed_by_last_sweep : UInt64
    def bytes_kept_by_last_sweep : UInt64
    # Bytes allocated since the last collection: the word the allocation
    # trigger reads, folded in per cache slice and reset by every
    # collection.
    def bytes_since_collection : UInt64
    # How many collections have run.
    def collections : UInt64
    def initialize(mapped_bytes : UInt64, bytes_since_collection : UInt64, bytes_freed_by_last_sweep : UInt64, bytes_kept_by_last_sweep : UInt64, collections : UInt64)
    # Bytes the arenas and large mappings hold from the machine. A
    # reservation, counted in whole mappings; not bytes in use.
    def mapped_bytes : UInt64
    def to_s : String
  end
  # Runs one collection now.
  def self.collect : Nil
  # The allocation trigger stops running collections until `enable`.
  def self.disable : Nil
  # The allocation trigger runs collections again. `collect` still works
  # while disabled.
  def self.enable : Nil
  # Hands a chunk back before the sweep would. A null pointer is nothing
  # to free.
  def self.free(pointer : ::Pointer(Void)) : Nil
  def initialize
  # Whether `pointer` points into a live chunk on the collector's heap:
  # its start or any byte inside it. Null, a stack address and a freed
  # chunk answer false.
  #
  # Under the runtime lock, as `stats` is: a word in no arena walks the
  # large-mapping list, and another thread's `free` or sweep unlinks and
  # unmaps those nodes under that lock. Walked without it, beside three
  # threads whose large chunks come and go, two seconds of `is_heap_ptr`
  # died of a memory fault in 10 runs of 10 (`bench/std_gc_exercise.iyi`).
  def self.is_heap_ptr(pointer : ::Pointer(Void)) : Bool
  # `size` zeroed bytes the collector scans for pointers. A negative size
  # is refused by name.
  def self.malloc(size : Int) : ::Pointer(Void)
  # `size` bytes the collector does not scan: for bytes that hold no
  # pointers, so the marker skips them. They are not cleared - a chunk the
  # sweep handed back comes out with its last owner's bytes, as Boehm's
  # `GC_malloc_atomic` hands them out - so the caller writes every byte
  # it reads. This said "zeroed" while 2000 chunks taken after a
  # collection freed 2000 filled ones came back dirty, every one.
  def self.malloc_atomic(size : Int) : ::Pointer(Void)
  # The chunk at `pointer`, resized to `size` bytes; the answer may be a
  # new address, with the old bytes copied.
  def self.realloc(pointer : ::Pointer(Void), size : Int) : ::Pointer(Void)
  # The numbers the collector keeps, read now.
  #
  # The walk holds the runtime lock, which a collection takes before it
  # stops anything and holds while the scavenge unlinks an arena or a
  # large mapping. Walked without it, a collection another thread's
  # allocation started could stop this walk on a mapping, unlink and unmap
  # it, and the walk's next read was of memory gone: beside three threads
  # allocating, two seconds of `stats` died of a memory fault in 10 runs
  # of 10 (`bench/std_gc_exercise.iyi`).
  def self.stats : Stats
end

surfaces.name: std/http
surfaces.stdout:
module std/http

pub struct HTTP
  # For a request target in absolute form (RFC 9112 §3.2.2), where its
  # authority starts: after `http://` or `https://`, in any case.
  def self.absolute_form(target : String) : Int32 | ::Nil
  # Where a chunked body that starts at *from* ends in `text` — the byte
  # after the last chunk's terminating CRLF (trailers included) — nil when
  # it has not all arrived, or why it is not a chunked body. What
  # `decode_chunked` will then read whole.
  def self.chunked_end(text : String, from : Int32 = 0) : Int32 | String | Nil
  # A `Content-Length` as a number, or nil when it is not one. Repeated
  # lines arrive joined, and are one length only when every one says the
  # same (RFC 9112 §6.3). A length past 2147483647 is still a length, too
  # large for either side, and is read as one past it: `to_i?` answered
  # nil for it, and 3000000000 was refused as "not a number".
  def self.content_length(value : String) : Int64 | ::Nil
  # A control character other than a tab, or DEL: what a field value may
  # not hold (RFC 9110 §5.5), nor a request target or a reason phrase.
  def self.control?(text : String) : Bool
  # A chunked body (RFC 9112 §7.1) as one string: each chunk's size line
  # is hexadecimal, extensions after `;` are ignored, and a zero-length
  # chunk ends it. What follows the last chunk is trailers, which nothing
  # here reads.
  def self.decode_chunked(text : String) : String
  def self.delete(url : String, headers : Hash(String, String) = {} of String => String) : Response | Cancelled | SocketError
  def self.find_headers_end(text : String, from : Int32 = 0) : Int32 | ::Nil
  # The request as it goes on the wire. `Host`, `Connection` and
  # `Content-Length` are the request's own lines; a caller's header of
  # that name is refused rather than sent twice. A body's length is
  # always written for the methods a body belongs to, so `POST` with
  # nothing to say still says `Content-Length: 0`. A byte of the path past
  # 127 goes as `%` and two hex digits: a request target is ASCII (RFC
  # 9112 §3.2, RFC 3986 §2.1), and `/ü` went out as its UTF-8 bytes, raw.
  def self.format_request(method : String, path : String, host : String, body : String = "", headers : Hash(String, String) = {} of String => String) : String
  def self.get(url : String, headers : Hash(String, String) = {} of String => String) : Response | Cancelled | SocketError
  def self.has_break?(text : String) : Bool
  # Whether a list of tokens (RFC 9110 §5.6.1), its repeated lines joined
  # with ", ", holds *token*, in any case.
  def self.has_token?(list : String, token : String) : Bool
  def self.head(url : String, headers : Hash(String, String) = {} of String => String) : Response | Cancelled | SocketError
  # A Host value - the `a` of `Host: a` - or an absolute-form target's
  # authority, made of what a host and its port are spelled with (RFC 3986
  # §3.2.2, §3.2.3): a name, an IPv4 address or an IPv6 one in brackets,
  # and digits after a colon. Empty is one too, for a target with no
  # authority (RFC 9112 §3.2). A blank, a `/`, an `@` - the bytes another
  # host or a path begins with - are not.
  def self.host?(text : String) : Bool
  def initialize
  # The field lines after the first, or why they are not fields. A name
  # repeated, in any case, is one field, its values joined in order with
  # ", " (RFC 9110 §5.3): into a Hash by name, a second line spelled the
  # same replaced the first and one spelled otherwise was an entry
  # `header` never reached, so two different `Content-Length`s were read
  # as whichever came first or last. A value with a control character in
  # it - a CR or LF that ends no line, a NUL - is refused (§5.5) rather than
  # handed to whoever reads it or echoes it into a header.
  #
  # *unfold*, for an answer: a line that begins with a blank continues the
  # field above it (obs-fold, RFC 9112 §5.2), and a user agent joins it on
  # with one space; read as a field of its own, `HTTP.get` panicked with
  # "header without a colon: \" b\"". A server may refuse one, and this
  # one does.
  #
  # *apart*, when given, is handed each repeated field's values by the
  # name in the answer, a line each, before they are joined.
  def self.parse_fields(lines : Array(String), unfold : Bool = false, apart : Hash(String, Array(String)) | ::Nil = nil) : Hash(String, String) | String
  # The response as it came off the wire. `head` says the request was a
  # `HEAD`, whose answer carries the headers of a body it does not send.
  # An interim answer - `100 Continue`, `103 Early Hints` - is read past to
  # the final one after it (RFC 9110 §15.2): the server here answers
  # `Expect: 100-continue` with a 100, and `HTTP.post` returned the 100.
  # A `101` switches protocols, and HTTP ends with it.
  def self.parse_response(text : String, head : Bool = false) : Response
  # Where *text* goes on at *from* past the empty lines there: what a
  # server skips before a request line (RFC 9112 §2.2).
  def self.past_empty_lines(text : String, from : Int32) : Int32
  def self.post(url : String, body : String = "", headers : Hash(String, String) = {} of String => String) : Response | Cancelled | SocketError
  def self.put(url : String, body : String = "", headers : Hash(String, String) = {} of String => String) : Response | Cancelled | SocketError
  # A chunked body as it arrives, from *from* in *held* and then what
  # *client* reads: the body and what came after it, the reason it is not
  # one, or nil when the connection ended first. Each read is decoded into
  # the body once; only an unfinished size line is carried to the next.
  def self.read_chunked(held : String, from : Int32, limit : Int32, &client : (-> String | ::Nil)) : ::Tuple(String, String) | String | Nil
  # A head as it arrives: *held*, then what *client* reads after it, until
  # a blank line at or after *from* ends a head, or more than *limit*
  # bytes after *from* hold none. The text, and where its head ends - nil
  # when *client* ran out first. Each read is searched once, with the three
  # bytes before it where a blank line may have begun, and kept in one
  # builder; a first read that holds a whole head is the text as it came.
  # Adding each read to the head so far and searching all of
  # what has arrived again cost the server 8.8 s for a 1 MB head that came
  # 128 bytes at a time, and 0.06 s for the same head in one piece.
  def self.read_head(held : String, from : Int32, limit : Int32, &client : (-> String | ::Nil)) : ::Tuple(String, Int32 | ::Nil)
  # The reason phrase a status carries (RFC 9110 §15), for a response the
  # server writes; a status this table does not know gets its class's.
  def self.reason_for(status : Int32) : String
  # One request, one answer, one connection, which `Connection: close`
  # asks the server to close. The answer is read as far as its framing
  # says (RFC 9112 §6.3) - its length, its last chunk, or its head alone
  # for a `HEAD`, a 1xx, 204 or 304 - and to the server's close only when it
  # has neither a length nor chunks. A head past `Server::MAX_HEAD`, the
  # megabyte the server takes of a request's, is refused. The socket parks
  # under the runtime, so a request from a task answers `Cancelled` when
  # the task is; a refused or reset connection answers `SocketError`; `!`
  # passes either up, `.or_panic` refuses it.
  def self.request(method : String, url : String, headers : Hash(String, String) = {} of String => String, body : String = "") : Response | Cancelled | SocketError
  # Two field names for the same field: ASCII case is the only difference
  # a name may carry.
  def self.same_name?(a : String, b : String) : Bool
  def self.split_crlf(text : String) : Array(String)
  # A token (RFC 9110 §5.6.2): what a method or a field name is made of.
  def self.token?(text : String) : Bool
  # Without the blanks at either end (RFC 9112 §5.1: field values are
  # trimmed of the whitespace around them).
  def self.trim(s : String) : String
end

# What a server's block is handed: one request, read whole.
pub struct Request
  def body : String
  def header(name : String) : String | ::Nil
  def headers : Hash(String, String)
  def initialize(method : String, path : String, query : String | ::Nil, headers : Hash(String, String), body : String)
  def method : String
  def path : String
  def query : String | ::Nil
end

pub struct Response
  def body : String
  # A header by name, as the server spelled it or otherwise: a field
  # name is case-insensitive (RFC 9110 §5.1), and `content-length` is as
  # common on the wire as `Content-Length`.
  def header(name : String) : String | ::Nil
  # A field's lines apart, in the order they came: `header` joins them
  # with ", ", and `Set-Cookie` is the field that join breaks (RFC 9110
  # §5.3), since a cookie's `Expires` date has a comma in it - two cookies
  # read as "a=1; Expires=Wed, 21 Oct 2026 07:28:00 GMT, b=2", which no
  # split takes back apart. Empty for a field that is not there.
  def header_values(name : String) : Array(String)
  def headers : Hash(String, String)
  def initialize(status : Int32, reason : String, headers : Hash(String, String), body : String, apart : Hash(String, Array(String)) | ::Nil = nil)
  # A response to write: the reason is the status's own, the headers the
  # caller's. `Response.new(200, "hello")` is the common shape.
  def initialize(status : Int32, body : String = "", headers : Hash(String, String) = {} of String => String)
  def reason : String
  def status : Int32
  def success? : Bool
  # The same answer with *body* for its body: the client reads a chunked
  # body after the head it parsed.
  protected def with_body(body : String) : Response
end

pub struct Server
  # The response as it goes on the wire. `Content-Length` is the body's
  # (or the caller's, for a HEAD that describes a body it does not send),
  # `Connection` says what the connection will do next. A 1xx, 204 or 304
  # has no content (RFC 9110 §15), and writes neither a body nor a length
  # of its own (§8.6): the body was read by the client as the start of the
  # next answer, and `Content-Length: 0` on a 304 told a cache that the
  # resource had become empty.
  def self.format_response(response : Response, head : Bool, close : Bool) : String
  # One connection: requests until the client is done. A request that is
  # not HTTP is answered 400 and the connection closed, since the bytes
  # after it cannot be trusted to be a request either.
  #
  # Under `serve`, *listener* and *idle*: every read waits with the
  # connection in *idle*, for `serve` to close once the listener is, and
  # none starts once the listener is closed (`wait_read`).
  def self.handle(client : IyiSocket, handler : Proc(Request, Response), listener : IyiSocket | ::Nil = nil, idle : Hash(UInt64, IyiSocket) | ::Nil = nil) : Nil
  def initialize
  # A request at *from* in `text`, if a whole one is there. No request and
  # no error means "not yet". `consumed` and `wanted` count from the start
  # of `text`: a server parses each request where it lies in
  # what has arrived, and copies none of what follows it.
  def self.parse_request(text : String, from : Int32 = 0) : ParsedRequest
  # Serve `listener` until it is closed. The block runs on the
  # connection's fiber, once per request; what it answers is written back.
  # The close ends a connection waiting on its client too, for its next
  # request or for the rest of one, and one that is answering ends when its
  # answer is written: a keep-alive client that sat idle kept `serve` from
  # returning for as long as it stayed, and so did one that had sent
  # what has arrived of a request so far - one byte of it was enough.
  def self.serve(listener : IyiSocket, &handler : (Request -> Response)) : Nil
end

surfaces.name: std/indexable
surfaces.stdout:
module std/indexable

pub trait Indexable
  type Elem
  # Returns the element at the given index. Negative indices count from the
  # end, so `a[-1]` returns the last element. Raises when index is out of
  # bounds, naming the index as it was written and the size there was:
  # `index out of range` on its own told a caller with a computed index
  # nothing it did not already know. The wording is `Array`'s
  # (src/iyi/array.iyi), because one mistake gets one sentence.
  def [](index : Int32) : Elem
  # Returns the element at the given index, or nil when index is out of bounds.
  # Negative indices count from the end.
  def []?(index : Int32) : Elem | ::Nil
  # Binary search on a sorted collection. Returns the first element for which
  # the block returns true, or nil if no element matches.
  def bsearch(& : (Elem -> Bool)) : Elem | ::Nil
  # Binary search returning the index of the first element for which the block
  # returns true, or nil.
  def bsearch_index(& : (Elem -> Bool)) : Int32 | ::Nil
  # Single-index navigation.
  def dig(index : Int32) : Elem
  # Single-index nilable navigation.
  def dig?(index : Int32) : Elem | ::Nil
  # Default iteration yielding elements sequentially from 0 up to size - 1.
  # It answers `Enumerable`'s requirement for a type that also says `impl
  # Enumerable`, which is one more line than the ergonomics claim implies
  # (SPEC.md II.6) — the claim that this trait supplied it was false, and
  # `Array` went without `zip`, `take` and the rest until the line existed.
  def each(& : (Elem -> Nil)) : Nil
  # Yields consecutive overlapping windows of n elements each.
  def each_cons(n : Int32, & : (Array(Elem) -> Nil)) : Nil
  # Returns an Array of consecutive overlapping windows of n elements each.
  def each_cons(n : Int32) : Array(Array(Elem))
  # Yields each valid index from 0 up to size - 1.
  def each_index(& : (Int32 -> Nil)) : Nil
  # Yields slices of n elements each to the given block.
  def each_slice(n : Int32, & : (Array(Elem) -> Nil)) : Nil
  # Returns an Array of slices of n elements each.
  def each_slice(n : Int32) : Array(Array(Elem))
  # Returns true when the collection contains no elements.
  def empty? : Bool
  # Structural equality comparing collection size and element values.
  def equals?(other : self) : Bool
  # Structural equality comparing elements with a custom predicate block.
  def equals?(other : self, & : (Elem, Elem -> Bool)) : Bool
  # Returns the element at index. If out of bounds, returns the default value.
  def fetch(index : Int32, default : Elem) : Elem
  # Returns the element at index. If out of bounds, yields the original index
  # to the given block and returns its result.
  def fetch(index : Int32, & : (Int32 -> Elem)) : Elem
  # Returns the first element. Raises when the collection is empty.
  def first : Elem
  # Returns the first element, or nil when the collection is empty.
  def first? : Elem | ::Nil
  # Combines the elements' hashes. Wrapping arithmetic, because a hash is a
  # number modulo the word and nothing else: written with the checked `*` and
  # `+`, this panicked with "arithmetic overflow" the moment a collection was
  # long enough for `31 * h` to leave `Int32` - six elements of two digits
  # each was enough, while the five-element cases in the gates passed.
  #
  # Mixed as the prelude's `Array#hash` is, which is also what keeps an
  # array's and another indexable's hashes one function: `31 * h + e` gave
  # a grid of pairs a few hashes between many, and a table probing a slot
  # at a time merged their runs.
  def hash : Int32
  # Returns the first index where element equals value, or nil if not found.
  def index(value : Elem) : Int32 | ::Nil
  # Returns the first index for which the block returns true, or nil.
  def index(& : (Elem -> Bool)) : Int32 | ::Nil
  # Joins element string representations with the specified separator.
  #
  # Into one builder, as `Array#join` writes: adding each element to the
  # text so far copied that text once per element, and 20,000 elements
  # took 1.8 s where the same array's `join` took 1 ms.
  def join(separator : String = "") : String
  # Returns the last element. Raises when the collection is empty.
  def last : Elem
  # Returns the last element, or nil when the collection is empty.
  def last? : Elem | ::Nil
  # Yields elements in reverse order, from size - 1 down to 0.
  def reverse_each(& : (Elem -> Nil)) : Nil
  # Returns the last index where element equals value, or nil if not found.
  def rindex(value : Elem) : Int32 | ::Nil
  # Returns the last index for which the block returns true, or nil.
  def rindex(& : (Elem -> Bool)) : Int32 | ::Nil
  # One element, or *n* distinct ones, chosen by `random`, a fresh generator
  # when none is given, the way std/random's `Array#sample` chooses them:
  # so a `Deque` makes the other library's choices in its order, as an
  # array does. `sample(Int32)` was a seed here and a count there, so
  # `[10, 20, 30, 40, 50].sample(3)` answered 20 without std/random and
  # three elements with it, a `Deque`'s answered 20 either way, and
  # `sample` answered the middle element on every run.
  def sample(random : Random | ::Nil = nil) : Elem
  def sample(n : Int32, random : Random | ::Nil = nil) : Array(Elem)
  # Returns a sample element using the index returned by the caller's block.
  def sample(& : (Int32 -> Int32)) : Elem
  abstract def size : Int32
  # Copies elements into a newly allocated Array with pre-allocated capacity.
  def to_a : Array(Elem)
  abstract def unsafe_fetch(index : Int32) : Elem
  # Returns an Array containing elements at the given indices array.
  def values_at(indexes : Array(Int32)) : Array(Elem)
  # Returns an Array containing elements at the given indices.
  def values_at(*indexes : Int32) : Array(Elem)
end

# `Indexable` with one more requirement, `unsafe_put`, from which the
# in-place operations follow. In-place variants are spelled `_in_place`;
# the copies (`rotated`, `reversed`) live on the concrete type, since a
# trait cannot build one without knowing how.
pub trait IndexableMutable : ::Std::Indexable::Indexable
  type Elem
  # The count elements from offset become value. A negative count is a
  # mistake; a window that runs past the end is refused by naming the
  # index that would have been written.
  def fill(value : Elem, offset : Int32, count : Int32) : self
  # Every element becomes value.
  def fill(value : Elem) : self
  # Every element becomes what the block answers for its index.
  def fill(& : (Int32 -> Elem)) : self
  # Reverses elements in place.
  def reverse_in_place : self
  # Rotates elements in place so that the element at position n comes
  # first; a negative n rotates the other way. Three reversals, no
  # scratch space.
  def rotate_in_place(n : Int32 = 1) : self
  # Swaps two elements in place.
  def swap(index0 : Int32, index1 : Int32) : self
  abstract def unsafe_put(index : Int32, value : Elem) : Elem
  # Replaces the element at index with what the block answers for it,
  # and answers the new value.
  def update(index : Int32, & : (Elem -> Elem)) : Elem
end

impl Indexable for Array(T) forall T
  def unsafe_fetch(index : Int32) : T
end

impl IndexableMutable for Array(T) forall T
  def unsafe_put(index : Int32, value : T) : T
end

class ::Array(T)
  # Every pair with an element of the other array, this array's order
  # first. Not `product`: on an `Enumerable`, `product` is the
  # multiplicative fold, and one name means one thing.
  def cartesian(other : Array(U)) : Array(Tuple(T, U)) forall U
  # Forgets every element.
  def clear : Array(T)
  # Removes the nils in place.
  def compact_in_place : Array(T)
  # Removes and answers the element at index, shifting what follows left.
  def delete_at(index : Int32) : T
  # Removes every element the block answers true for, in place, keeping
  # the order of the rest; one pass, no per-element shifting.
  def delete_if(& : (T -> Bool)) : Array(T)
  # The same pairs, handed to a block in the same order, with no array of
  # them made - the other library's `each_cartesian`.
  def each_cartesian(other : Array(U), & : (T, U -> _)) : Nil forall U
  # Inserts value at index, shifting what follows right. An index of
  # `size` appends; `-1` also appends, as the position after the last.
  def insert(index : Int32, value : T) : Array(T)
  # Keeps only the elements the block answers true for, in place.
  def keep_if(& : (T -> Bool)) : Array(T)
  # A copy rotated so that the element at position n comes first; the
  # past participle names the copy, as `sorted` and `reversed` do, and
  # `rotate_in_place` is the one that moves this array.
  def rotated(n : Int32 = 1) : Array(T)
end
